arml-2018-team-01.title: Split by the factorization of 18
arml-2018-team-01.body:
Both $|S|$ and $\max S$ are positive integers, so $(|S|,\max S)$ is one of $(1,18),(2,9),(3,6),(6,3),(9,2),(18,1)$. A set with largest element $m$ has at most $m$ elements, so the last three are impossible.

- $|S|=1$, $\max S=18$: only $\{18\}$ — **1** set.
- $|S|=2$, $\max S=9$: $\{a,9\}$ with $1\le a\le 8$ — **8** sets.
- $|S|=3$, $\max S=6$: choose the other two elements from $\{1,\dots,5\}$: $\binom52=$ **10** sets.

Total $1+8+10=19$.

**Answer: 19**

arml-2018-team-01.title: General formula
arml-2018-team-01.body:
For fixed $k=|S|$ and $m=\max S$, the number of sets is $\binom{m-1}{k-1}$ (choose the other $k-1$ elements below $m$). Summing over $km=18$:
$$\binom{17}{0}+\binom{8}{1}+\binom{5}{2}+\binom{2}{5}+\binom{1}{8}+\binom{0}{17}=1+8+10+0+0+0=19.$$

**Answer: 19**

arml-2018-team-02.title: Force the median to 0
arml-2018-team-02.body:
With 218 scores, the median is the average of the 109th and 110th scores in sorted order. Make it $0$ with exactly $110$ zeros, and make the other $108$ scores as large as possible, $100$. Then the mean is $\frac{108\cdot100}{218}=\frac{5400}{109}\approx 49.54$ and the difference is $\frac{5400}{109}$.

**Why this is best.** Let the median be $m$. At least $109$ scores are at most $m$, and the other $109$ are at most $100$, so the mean is at most $\frac{109m+10900}{218}=\frac{m+100}{2}$ and
$$\text{mean}-m\le\frac{100-m}{2}.$$
- If $m\ge1$ this is at most $49.5<\frac{5400}{109}$.
- If $m=\frac12$, the 109th and 110th scores are $0$ and $1$; the best case has $109$ zeros, one $1$ and $108$ hundreds: mean $\frac{10801}{218}$, difference $\frac{10801}{218}-\frac12=\frac{10692}{218}<\frac{10800}{218}$.
- If $m=0$, at least $110$ scores are $0$, which is the configuration above.

So the maximum is $\frac{5400}{109}$.

**Answer: $\frac{5400}{109}$**

arml-2018-team-03.title: Two cones minus two cones
arml-2018-team-03.body:
$RE$ is a short diagonal of the hexagon, $RE=6\sqrt3$, and the sides $RA$ and $EG$ are both perpendicular to $RE$. So the solid is symmetric about the plane through $N$ (and $S$) perpendicular to $RE$, and it consists of two congruent conic frustums meeting along the circle traced by $N$.

Let $O$ be the midpoint of $RE$ (so $O$ lies on segment $SN$ with $OS=3$, $ON=12-3=9$), and extend $NA$ to meet line $RE$ at $P$. Triangle $PON$ has a $30^\circ$ angle at $P$, so $OP=9\sqrt3$, and $RP=6\sqrt3$ (indeed $OR=3\sqrt3$).

Revolving triangle $PON$ gives a cone of radius $9$ and height $9\sqrt3$; revolving the part beyond $RA$ (triangle $PRA$, radius $RA=6$, height $6\sqrt3$) gives a smaller cone. One frustum has volume
$$\tfrac13\pi\cdot 9^2\cdot 9\sqrt3-\tfrac13\pi\cdot6^2\cdot6\sqrt3=\tfrac13\pi\sqrt3(729-216)=171\sqrt3\,\pi.$$
The solid is two such frustums: $342\sqrt3\,\pi$, so $k=342\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $342\sqrt3$**

arml-2018-team-03.title: Pappus's centroid theorem
arml-2018-team-03.body:
Put $R=(0,0)$ and $E=(6\sqrt3,0)$ with the axis along $RE$. The pentagon $RANGE$ lies on one side of the axis with vertices $R(0,0)$, $A(0,6)$, $N(3\sqrt3,9)$, $G(6\sqrt3,6)$, $E(6\sqrt3,0)$ (distance from axis $=y$).

Split it into the rectangle $RAGE$ ($6\sqrt3\times6$, area $36\sqrt3$, centroid height $3$) and triangle $ANG$ (base $AG=6\sqrt3$, height $3$, area $9\sqrt3$, centroid height $6+1=7$).

By Pappus, volume $=2\pi\sum(\text{area}\times\text{centroid height})=2\pi(36\sqrt3\cdot3+9\sqrt3\cdot7)=2\pi\cdot171\sqrt3=342\sqrt3\,\pi$.

**Answer: $342\sqrt3$**

arml-2018-team-04.title: Quadratic in tan θ
arml-2018-team-04.body:
Let $u=\tan\theta$. Then $\frac{2u}{1-u^2}=\frac xy$, i.e. $xu^2+2yu-x=0$. Its discriminant is $4y^2+4x^2$, so $u$ is rational iff $x^2+y^2$ is a perfect square.

Pythagorean triples with both legs at most 12: $(3,4,5),(6,8,10),(9,12,15),(5,12,13)$. So the good ordered pairs are $(3,4),(4,3),(6,8),(8,6),(9,12),(12,9),(5,12),(12,5)$ — 8 of the 144 outcomes.

Probability $\frac{8}{144}=\frac1{18}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{18}$**

arml-2018-team-04.title: Geometric view
arml-2018-team-04.body:
$\tan2\theta=\frac xy$ with $2\theta\in(0,\pi)$ means $2\theta$ is the angle of the vector $(y,x)$. Then $\tan\theta=\frac{\sin2\theta}{1+\cos2\theta}=\frac{x/r}{1+y/r}=\frac{x}{r+y}$ where $r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$. This is rational iff $r$ is rational, i.e. iff $x^2+y^2$ is a perfect square. Counting as before gives $8$ of $144$ outcomes, probability $\frac1{18}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{18}$**

arml-2018-team-06.title: Find the pieces of S
arml-2018-team-06.body:
$x,y$ can't both be integers (the products would be equal).

**Exactly one integer.** If $x$ is an integer and $\lfloor y\rfloor=b$, then $x(b+1)=20$, $xb=18$, so $x=2$, $b=9$: the open vertical segment $\{2\}\times(9,10)$. (Multiplying gives $x^2b(b+1)=360$; only $x^2=4$ works, and $x=-2$ fails.) Symmetrically, $y=-2$ with $-10<x<-9$: the open horizontal segment $(-10,-9)\times\{-2\}$.

**Neither an integer.** With $\lfloor x\rfloor=a$, $\lfloor y\rfloor=b$: $a(b+1)=20$ and $(a+1)b=18$. Then $a(a+1)b(b+1)=360=3\cdot4\cdot5\cdot6$, and checking the candidates leaves $(a,b)=(5,3)$ and $(-4,-6)$: the open unit squares $(5,6)\times(3,4)$ and $(-4,-3)\times(-6,-5)$.

**Farthest pair.** The supremum of distances is attained between extreme corner/end points (not included, hence "least upper bound"):
- segment to segment: $(-10,-2)$ to $(2,10)$: $\sqrt{288}$;
- square to square: $(6,4)$ to $(-4,-6)$: $\sqrt{200}$;
- segment to square: $(-10,-2)$ to $(6,4)$: $\sqrt{16^2+6^2}=\sqrt{292}$ (same by symmetry for $(2,10)$ and $(-4,-6)$).

The largest is $\sqrt{292}=2\sqrt{73}$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt{73}$**

arml-2018-team-07.title: Extended Law of Sines
arml-2018-team-07.body:
$A,B,C$ lie on the circle of radius $\sqrt d$ centered at the origin, so $AC=2\sqrt d\sin\angle ABC$, i.e. $\csc\angle ABC=\frac{2\sqrt d}{AC}$. We want $AC$ small and $d$ small.

- $AC=1$ is impossible: if $A=(x,y)$, $C=(x+1,y)$ then $x^2=(x+1)^2$, so $x=-\frac12$.
- $AC=\sqrt2$: WLOG $C=(x+1,y+1)$; equal distances give $x+y+1=0$, so $d=x^2+(x+1)^2$ and $\csc\angle ABC=\sqrt{2d}=\sqrt{2(x^2+(x+1)^2)}$. This exceeds $2018$ iff $x^2+(x+1)^2>2018^2/2=2036162$; the least such $x\ge0$ is $x=1009$ ($1009^2+1010^2=2038181$, while $1008^2+1009^2=2034145$). So $d=2038181$.
- $AC\ge\sqrt3$: then $2018<\frac{2\sqrt d}{\sqrt3}$, so $d>\frac34\cdot2018^2=3054243>2038181$.

$d=2038181$ is achieved by $A=(1009,1010)$, $C=(1010,1009)$, $B=(-1009,-1010)$.

**Answer: 2038181**

arml-2018-team-08.title: Four dissection shapes
arml-2018-team-08.body:
Any dissection of a rectangle into three rectangles has one full cut; the other two pieces come from cutting one side again. Up to symmetry there are four shapes:

1. three strips of height 3 (cuts parallel to the side of length 3);
2. three strips of width 5 (cuts parallel to the side of length 5);
3. one full-length strip $5\times h$ and the remaining $5\times(3-h)$ part cut into two by a cut of length $3-h$;
4. one strip $w\times3$ and the remaining $(5-w)\times3$ part cut into two by a cut of length $5-w$.

**Case 1.** Each strip is determined by its area, so a collection is a multiset of areas $a\le b\le c$ with $a+b+c=15$, i.e. a partition of 15 into 3 positive parts. Writing $a=x+1$, $b=a+y$, $c=b+z$ ($x,y,z\ge0$) gives $3x+2y+z=12$; counting by $x=0,1,2,3,4$ gives $7+5+4+2+1=19$.

**Case 2.** Same count: $19$.

**Case 3.** Let the top strip have area $15-n$ ($1\le n\le14$). The remaining rectangle of area $n$ is cut into two pieces with integer areas $k$ and $n-k$, which can be done in $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ unordered ways, and the top piece (with a side 5) never matches a lower piece in shape. Total $\sum_{n=1}^{14}\lfloor n/2\rfloor=49$.

**Case 4.** Similarly with a side strip of area $15-n$, but exclude $n=9$ (left piece $2\times3$): then the right part is $3\times3$ and its two pieces together with the left piece are already counted in Case 2 (rotate the $3\times3$ block). Total $49-\lfloor 9/2\rfloor=45$.

Comparing how many sides of length 5 appear shows the cases are otherwise disjoint. Total $19+19+49+45=132$.

**Answer: 132**

arml-2018-team-08.title: Computer check
arml-2018-team-08.body:
Enumerate all guillotine dissections: a first cut at position $c$ along either side with integer area of the first piece, then a second cut of the remaining rectangle in either direction with integer areas. Record each collection as a sorted multiset of (sorted) side-length pairs and count distinct multisets. This gives exactly $132$ collections, confirming the case analysis.

**Answer: 132**

arml-2018-team-09.title: Homothety, power of a point, antipodes
arml-2018-team-09.body:
Since $AD=AB+BC+CD$, the points $A,B,C,D$ are collinear in that order.

The homothety at $Y$ with ratio 2 maps $\gamma$ to $\Gamma$. Extend $YB$, $YC$ to meet $\Gamma$ at $P$, $Q$; then $B$, $C$ are midpoints of $YP$, $YQ$. Power of $B$ with respect to $\Gamma$: $AB\cdot BD=PB\cdot BY=BY^2$, so $BY^2=1\cdot6$, $BY=\sqrt6$. Similarly $CY^2=CA\cdot CD=5\cdot2$, $CY=\sqrt{10}$. Since $BY^2+CY^2=16=BC^2$, $\angle BYC=90^\circ$.

Let $S$ be the antipode of $B$ on $\omega_1$. Then $\angle BYS=90^\circ$, so $S$ lies on line $CY$, and $\angle BAS=90^\circ$. Triangles $CYB$ and $CAS$ are similar (right angles at $Y$ and $A$, common angle $C$), so $AS=\frac{YB}{YC}\cdot AC=\sqrt{\tfrac6{10}}\cdot5=\sqrt{15}$ and the diameter of $\omega_1$ is $BS=\sqrt{AS^2+AB^2}=\sqrt{16}=4$.

Likewise with $T$ the antipode of $C$ on $\omega_2$: $DT=\frac{YC}{YB}\cdot BD=\sqrt{\tfrac{10}6}\cdot6=\sqrt{60}$, so $CT=\sqrt{60+4}=8$.

The radii are $2$ and $4$, so the total area is $\pi(4+16)=20\pi$.

**Answer: $20\pi$**

arml-2018-team-10.title: Use rows 3 and 4
arml-2018-team-10.body:
From the figure, label the cells
$$\begin{array}{cccc}A&B&C&D\\A&B&Y&D\\W&B&Y&Z\\W&X&Y&Z\end{array}$$
(eight regions, eight different digits).

**Step 1 (row 4 is the average).** $3\cdot\overline{WXYZ}=\overline{ABCD}+\overline{ABYD}+\overline{WBYZ}$ rearranges to
$$0=2000(A-W)+300(B-X)+10(C-Y)+2(D-Z).$$
The last three terms are at most $2700+90+18<4000$ in size, so $A-W=\pm1$; then the rest forces $B-X=\mp7$, $C-Y=\pm9$, $D-Z=\pm5$ (same sign pattern). In particular $\{C,Y\}=\{0,9\}$.

**Step 2 (row 3 mod 10).** $4^x$ ends in 4 or 6, $5^y$ in 5, $31^z$ in 1, so row 3 ends in $0$ or $2$: $Z\in\{0,2\}$. Since one of $C,Y$ is $0$, $Z=2$, so $D=7$ and the signs are $A-W=-1$, $B-X=-7$, $C-Y=9$: $C=9$, $Y=0$.

**Step 3.** $B-X=-7$ with $0,2$ used gives $B=1$, $X=8$. Row 3 is $\overline{W102}=4^x+5^y+31^z$. Mod 10 forces $x$ even (so $x\ge2$ and $8\mid 4^x$); then mod 8, $5^y+31^z\equiv 102\equiv 6\pmod 8$ forces $y$ odd, $z$ even, so $z=2$ ($31^4$ is too big). Then $4^x+5^y\equiv 141\pmod{1000}$ with $x\le6$ even and $y\le5$ odd forces $x=2$ and $y\in\{3,5\}$; $y=3$ gives $W=1=B$, so $y=5$: $16+3125+961=4102$, $W=4$, and $A=5$.

The grid:
$$\begin{array}{cccc}5&1&9&7\\5&1&0&7\\4&1&0&2\\4&8&0&2\end{array}$$
Check: $5197=4^4+13^3+14^3$, $5107=5^2+13^2+17^3$, $4102=4^2+5^5+31^2$, and $(5197+5107+4102)/3=4802$.

**Answer: rows 5197, 5107, 4102, 4802**

arml-2018-team-10.title: Exhaustive check
arml-2018-team-10.body:
List all four-digit values of each clue (exponents are small since $4^7>9999$, $13^4>9999$, etc.), then try every assignment of eight distinct digits to the regions $A,B,C,D,W,X,Y,Z$ (leading digits nonzero) and test the four row conditions. Exactly one assignment works: rows $5197$, $5107$, $4102$, $4802$.

**Answer: rows 5197, 5107, 4102, 4802**
